method: The mean solar day is divided into 1,000 equal .beats, so one .beat is 86,400 / 1,000 = 86.4 seconds and an hour is 1,000 / 24 = 41 2/3 beats. Biel Mean Time is a fixed UTC+1 offset with no daylight saving, so an instant's beat is floor(((UTC milliseconds + 3,600,000) modulo 86,400,000) / 86,400), which runs 0 to 999, and the remainder of that division is how far into the current beat the instant falls. The next beat starts 86,400 minus that remainder milliseconds later. A .beat names a time of day and not a date, so the reverse panel takes the BMT date: the UTC instant of BMT midnight is that calendar date at 00:00 minus one hour, and the beat adds beat x 86,400 ms to it. Because @000 is 23:00 UTC, every beat below 41 2/3 lands on the previous UTC date, and the page says so when that happens. A watch shows whole beats, so the headline floors the fraction, while the exact quotient is reported to three decimals and clock times to 0.1 s, far finer than the 86.4 s beat. This is the fixed-offset civil scale Swatch defined, not mean solar time measured at Biel, and leap seconds are ignored.

sources.title: Swatch Internet Time - Wikipedia: 1,000 .beats to the mean solar day, 86.4 seconds per beat, and Biel Mean Time as a year-round UTC+1 that never observes daylight saving
